claim: MakA is part of the MakA/B/E tripartite toxin involved in membrane pore formation similar to other α-PFTs.
source: As part of the MakA/B/E tripartite toxin, MakA is involved in membrane pore formation similar to other α-PFTs.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known function of MakA when part of the tripartite complex.

claim: MakA in isolation induces tube-like structures in acidic endosomal compartments of epithelial cells in vitro.
source: In contrast, MakA in isolation induces tube-like structures in acidic endosomal compartments of epithelial cells in vitro.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: MakA tubular growth occurs in a pH-, lipid-, and concentration-dependent manner.
source: The present study unravels the dynamics of tubular growth, which occurs in a pH-, lipid-, and concentration-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through multiple experiments in the manuscript.

claim: Within acidified organelle lumens or when incubated with cells in acidic media, MakA forms oligomers and remodels membranes into high-curvature tubes leading to loss of membrane integrity.
source: Within acidified organelle lumens or when incubated with cells in acidic media, MakA forms oligomers and remodels membranes into high-curvature tubes leading to loss of membrane integrity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data including Western blots, microscopy, and cell toxicity assays.

claim: A 3.7 Å cryo-electron microscopy structure of MakA filaments reveals a unique protein-lipid superstructure.
source: A 3.7 Å cryo-electron microscopy structure of MakA filaments reveals a unique protein-lipid superstructure.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through cryo-EM structural analysis.

claim: MakA forms a pinecone-like spiral with a central cavity and a thin annular lipid bilayer embedded between the MakA transmembrane helices in its active α-PFT conformation.
source: MakA forms a pinecone-like spiral with a central cavity and a thin annular lipid bilayer embedded between the MakA transmembrane helices in its active α-PFT conformation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through cryo-EM structural analysis.

claim: Pore-forming toxins can be categorized into two main groups, α-PFTs and β-PFTs, based on whether the secondary structure of the membrane-penetrating domain contains α-helices or β-barrels, respectively.
source: PFTs can be categorized into two main groups, α-PFTs and β-PFTs, based on whether the secondary structure of the membrane-penetrating domain contains α-helices or β-barrels, respectively (Los et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Los et al., 2013.

claim: PFTs are generally secreted from bacteria in a monomeric, soluble form.
source: Generally, PFTs are secreted from bacteria in a monomeric, soluble form.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about PFTs in the introduction.

claim: Upon recognition and binding to the target cell membrane, PFT toxins undergo a conformational change, interact with the membrane, dimerize, and oligomerize, leading to the formation of membrane pores.
source: Upon recognition and binding to the target cell membrane, the toxins undergo a conformational change, interact with the membrane, dimerize, and oligomerize, leading to the formation of membrane pores (Bischofberger et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bischofberger et al., 2012.

claim: Vibrio cholerae is a Gram-negative bacterium that is the causal organism of the diarrheal disease cholera.
source: Vibrio cholerae, a Gram-negative bacterium, is the causal organism of the diarrheal disease cholera (Clemens et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Clemens et al., 2017.

claim: Cholera toxin (CT) and toxin co-regulated pilus (TCP) are the main virulence factors of V. cholerae that cause disease in mammalian hosts.
source: Cholera toxin (CT) and toxin co-regulated pilus (TCP) are the main virulence factors of V. cholerae that cause disease in mammalian hosts (Kaper et al., 1994; Taylor et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kaper et al., 1994 and Taylor et al., 1987.

claim: Most environmental V. cholerae isolates do not produce CT and TCP.
source: Most environmental V. cholerae isolates do not produce CT and TCP (Rajpara et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rajpara et al., 2013.

claim: Environmental V. cholerae bacteria are considered pathogenic since they have been associated with secretory diarrhea and may cause wound infections and sepsis.
source: Nevertheless, these bacteria are considered pathogenic since they have been associated with secretory diarrhea and may cause wound infections and sepsis (Schwartz et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schwartz et al., 2019.

claim: V. cholerae strains lacking the CT-encoding genes often contain a set of genes coding for other secreted virulence factors, including hemolysin, hemagglutinin protease, RTX toxin, and multiple lipases.
source: V. cholerae strains lacking the CT-encoding genes often contain a set of genes coding for other secreted virulence factors, including hemolysin, hemagglutinin protease, RTX toxin, and multiple lipases that together may play a role in pathogenesis (Schwartz et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Schwartz et al., 2019.

claim: Using Caenorhabditis elegans and Danio rerio (zebrafish) as host models, evidence was obtained for a new V. cholerae cytotoxin denoted MakA (motility-associated killing factor A).
source: Using Caenorhabditis elegans and Danio rerio (zebrafish) as host models for bacterial predatory interactions and infection in aqueous environments, respectively, we obtained evidence for a new V. cholerae cytotoxin denoted MakA (motility-associated killing factor A) (Dongre et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dongre et al., 2018.

claim: The V. cholerae gene makA (vca0883) is localized in a gene cluster together with makC (vca0881), makD (vca0880), makB (vca0882), and makE (vca0884).
source: The V. cholerae gene makA (vca0883) is localized in a gene cluster together with makC (vca0881), makD (vca0880), makB (vca0882), and makE (vca0884).
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the genetic organization of the mak genes.

claim: The mak gene cluster has been found in different V. cholerae strains, including CT-negative isolates.
source: This gene cluster has been found in different V. cholerae strains, including CT-negative isolates (Dongre et al., 2018; Nadeem et al., 2021c; Tsou and Zhu, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dongre et al., 2018; Nadeem et al., 2021c; and Tsou and Zhu, 2010.

claim: The crystal structure of MakA revealed that it belongs to the ClyA α-PFT family.
source: The crystal structure of MakA revealed that it belongs to the ClyA α-PFT family (Dongre et al., 2018), named after the potent, one-component, PFT ClyA which is expressed from a monocistronic operon in Escherichia coli (Oscarsson et al., 1999; Oscarsson et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dongre et al., 2018; Oscarsson et al., 1999; and Oscarsson et al., 1996.

claim: MakA can form a tripartite cytolytic complex with MakB and MakE.
source: Our recent studies of the proteins encoded by the mak genes in V. cholerae demonstrated that MakA can form a tripartite cytolytic complex with MakB and MakE, whereas neither of the three proteins displays cytolytic activity on their own (Nadeem et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nadeem et al., 2021a.

claim: Neither MakA, MakB, nor MakE displays cytolytic activity on their own.
source: Our recent studies of the proteins encoded by the mak genes in V. cholerae demonstrated that MakA can form a tripartite cytolytic complex with MakB and MakE, whereas neither of the three proteins displays cytolytic activity on their own (Nadeem et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nadeem et al., 2021a.

claim: Other family members of α-PFT are found among the bipartite toxins from Yersinia enterocolitica (YaxAB) and Xenorhabdus nematophila (XaxAB).
source: Other family members of α-PFT are found among the bipartite toxins from Yersinia enterocolitica (YaxAB) and Xenorhabdus nematophila (XaxAB) (Brauning et al., 2018; Schubert et al., 2018), as well as among the tripartite toxins from Bacillus cereus (NheABC and HblL1L2B) (Sastalla et al., 2013), Aeromonas hydrophila (AhlABC) (Wilson et al., 2019), and Serratia marcescens (SmhABC) (Churchill-Angus et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brauning et al., 2018 and Schubert et al., 2018.

claim: Tripartite α-PFT toxins are found in Bacillus cereus (NheABC and HblL1L2B), Aeromonas hydrophila (AhlABC), and Serratia marcescens (SmhABC).
source: Other family members of α-PFT are found among the bipartite toxins from Yersinia enterocolitica (YaxAB) and Xenorhabdus nematophila (XaxAB) (Brauning et al., 2018; Schubert et al., 2018), as well as among the tripartite toxins from Bacillus cereus (NheABC and HblL1L2B) (Sastalla et al., 2013), Aeromonas hydrophila (AhlABC) (Wilson et al., 2019), and Serratia marcescens (SmhABC) (Churchill-Angus et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sastalla et al., 2013; Wilson et al., 2019; and Churchill-Angus et al., 2021.

claim: Bipartite and tripartite PFTs require the combined action of all protein partners to induce pore formation in the target membranes.
source: The bipartite and tripartite PFTs require the combined action of all protein partners to induce pore formation in the target membranes, and there is evidence that protein interaction occurs in a specific order for maximum cytolytic activity (Churchill-Angus et al., 2021; Nadeem et al., 2021c; Wilson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Churchill-Angus et al., 2021; Nadeem et al., 2021c; and Wilson et al., 2019.

claim: Protein interaction in bipartite and tripartite PFTs occurs in a specific order for maximum cytolytic activity.
source: The bipartite and tripartite PFTs require the combined action of all protein partners to induce pore formation in the target membranes, and there is evidence that protein interaction occurs in a specific order for maximum cytolytic activity (Churchill-Angus et al., 2021; Nadeem et al., 2021c; Wilson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Churchill-Angus et al., 2021; Nadeem et al., 2021c; and Wilson et al., 2019.

claim: An equimolar mixture of the MakA, MakB, and MakE proteins efficiently could assemble into a pore-forming complex in mammalian membranes.
source: We recently demonstrated that an equimolar mixture of the MakA, MakB, and MakE proteins efficiently could assemble into a pore-forming complex in mammalian membranes (Nadeem et al., 2021c).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nadeem et al., 2021c.

claim: Secretion of the MakA/B/E proteins from V. cholerae was shown to be facilitated via the bacterial flagellum.
source: Secretion of the MakA/B/E proteins from V. cholerae was shown to be facilitated via the bacterial flagellum (Dongre et al., 2018; Nadeem et al., 2021c).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dongre et al., 2018 and Nadeem et al., 2021c.

claim: About 10% of MakA was secreted from V. cholerae lacking the flagellum suggesting an alternative route of secretion.
source: However, about 10% of MakA was secreted from V. cholerae lacking the flagellum suggesting an alternative route of secretion, in contrast to MakB and MakE, which displayed a more definitive flagellum-dependent secretion (Dongre et al., 2018; Nadeem et al., 2021c).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dongre et al., 2018 and Nadeem et al., 2021c.

claim: MakB and MakE displayed a more definitive flagellum-dependent secretion compared to MakA.
source: However, about 10% of MakA was secreted from V. cholerae lacking the flagellum suggesting an alternative route of secretion, in contrast to MakB and MakE, which displayed a more definitive flagellum-dependent secretion (Dongre et al., 2018; Nadeem et al., 2021c).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dongre et al., 2018 and Nadeem et al., 2021c.

claim: Purified MakA protein binds to the target cell membrane and, upon internalization, may accumulate in the endolysosomal membrane.
source: Our earlier studies with purified MakA protein and cultured mammalian cells showed that the protein binds to the target cell membrane and, upon internalization, may accumulate in the endolysosomal membrane, causing lysosomal dysfunction, modulation of autophagy, and apoptotic cell death (Corkery et al., 2021; Nadeem et al., 2021a; Nadeem et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Corkery et al., 2021; Nadeem et al., 2021a; and Nadeem et al., 2021b.

claim: MakA accumulation in the endolysosomal membrane causes lysosomal dysfunction, modulation of autophagy, and apoptotic cell death.
source: Our earlier studies with purified MakA protein and cultured mammalian cells showed that the protein binds to the target cell membrane and, upon internalization, may accumulate in the endolysosomal membrane, causing lysosomal dysfunction, modulation of autophagy, and apoptotic cell death (Corkery et al., 2021; Nadeem et al., 2021a; Nadeem et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Corkery et al., 2021; Nadeem et al., 2021a; and Nadeem et al., 2021b.

claim: Cell membrane dynamics are crucial for various biological processes in all kingdoms of life.
source: Cell membrane dynamics are crucial for various biological processes in all kingdoms of life.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge in the introduction.

claim: In eukaryotes, the lipid bilayer and the number of membrane-associated proteins play a crucial role in the regulation of endocytosis, exocytosis, cell motility, cytokinesis, and maintenance of the organelle function in living cells.
source: In eukaryotes, the lipid bilayer and the number of membrane-associated proteins play a crucial role in the regulation of endocytosis, exocytosis, cell motility, cytokinesis, and maintenance of the organelle function in living cells (Tanaka-Takiguchi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tanaka-Takiguchi et al., 2013.

claim: The major proteins that play a key role in the regulation of endocytosis and intracellular trafficking include F-BAR, ESCRT-III, and dynamin proteins.
source: The major proteins that play a key role in the regulation of endocytosis and intracellular trafficking include F-BAR, ESCRT-III, and dynamin proteins.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge in the introduction.

claim: In vitro, F-BAR, ESCRT-III, and dynamin proteins may associate with lipid membranes and generate spiral filaments, causing the lipid membranes to distort and form tubular assemblies.
source: In vitro, these proteins may associate with lipid membranes and generate spiral filaments, causing the lipid membranes to distort and form tubular assemblies (McCullough et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McCullough et al., 2018.

claim: A bacterial protein designated BdpA (BAR domain-like protein A) with BAR domain-like activity was identified in the Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 strain.
source: Recently, a bacterial protein designated BdpA (BAR domain-like protein A) with BAR domain-like activity was identified in the Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 strain.
evidence: This is stated as a recent finding in the introduction.

claim: BdpA forms redox-active membrane vesicles and micrometer-scale outer membrane extensions.
source: BdpA forms redox-active membrane vesicles and micrometer-scale outer membrane extensions (Phillips et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Phillips et al., 2021.

claim: Dynamin was previously shown to be associated with the lipid membrane in vitro and form a helical tube-like assembly.
source: In addition to BAR domain proteins, dynamin was previously shown to be associated with the lipid membrane in vitro and form a helical tube-like assembly (Sweitzer and Hinshaw, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sweitzer and Hinshaw, 1998.

claim: Bacterial dynamin-like proteins (BDLPs), like eukaryotic dynamin proteins, are well known for their capacity to induce tube assembly in the presence of lipid membranes.
source: Bacterial dynamin-like proteins (BDLPs), like eukaryotic dynamin proteins, are well known for their capacity to induce tube assembly in the presence of lipid membranes (Low and Löwe, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Low and Löwe, 2006.

claim: There are only a few known bacterial toxins that produce invaginations in lipid membranes and eukaryotic cells, which can be exploited to transport these toxins intracellularly.
source: Notably, there are only a few known bacterial toxins that produce invaginations in lipid membranes and eukaryotic cells, which can be exploited to transport these toxins intracellularly (Berg Klenow et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Berg Klenow et al., 2020.

claim: Upon treatment of Caco-2 cells with MakA (250 nM, 18 hr), co-localization of Alexa568-labeled MakA with GFP-LAMP1 or lysotracker in tubular structures was observed.
source: Upon treatment of Caco-2 cells with MakA (250 nM, 18 hr), we observed co-localization of the Alexa568-labeled MakA (Alexa568-MakA) with GFP-LAMP1 or lysotracker in tubular structures (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by confocal microscopy images in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Tubulation in the lysosomes was confirmed by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) of lysosomes isolated from MakA-treated HCT8 cells.
source: The tubulation in the lysosomes was further confirmed by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) of lysosomes isolated from MakA-treated HCT8 cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by TEM images in Figure 1B.

claim: Western blot analysis of lysosomes isolated from MakA-treated HCT8 and Caco-2 cells revealed the formation of dimeric, tetrameric, and oligomeric MakA complexes in addition to the MakA monomer.
source: Western blot analysis of lysosomes isolated from MakA-treated (250nM, 18 hr) HCT8 and Caco-2 cells revealed, in addition to the MakA monomer, the formation of dimeric, tetrameric, and oligomeric MakA complexes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Both confocal microscopy and TEM analysis revealed aggregation and tubulation of purified lysosomes exposed to native MakA or Alexa568-MakA at pH 5.0.
source: Both confocal microscopy and TEM analysis revealed aggregation and tubulation of lysosomes at pH 5.0 (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by microscopy images in Figure 1C and D.

claim: A majority of the lysosomes showed well-organized tubulation when exposed to MakA at pH 6.5.
source: In addition, a majority of the lysosomes showed well-organized tubulation when exposed to MakA at pH 6.5 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by TEM images in Figure 1D.

claim: No MakA-induced tubular structures were observed in lysosomes at pH 7.0.
source: In contrast, we did not observe any MakA-induced tubular structures in lysosomes at pH 7.0 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by TEM images in Figure 1D.

claim: Western blot analysis confirmed pH-dependent binding of MakA to lysosomes.
source: Western blot analysis confirmed pH-dependent binding of MakA to lysosomes (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by Western blot data in Figure 1E.

claim: Alexa568-MakA was shown to bind epithelial cells in a pH-dependent manner.
source: Alexa568-MakA was subsequently shown to bind epithelial cells in a pH-dependent manner (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by confocal microscopy images and quantification in Figure 1F and G.

claim: Accumulation of Alexa568-MakA on the plasma membrane, including filipodia-rich tubular structures, was observed in a time-dependent manner.
source: Consistent with our earlier findings (Nadeem et al., 2021a), we observed accumulation of Alexa568-MakA on the plasma membrane, including filipodia-rich tubular structures, in a time-dependent manner (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by live-cell imaging in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D, and consistent with previous work cited as Nadeem et al., 2021a.

claim: The time scale of MakA binding to individual HCT8 cells ranged from ~40 min to 4 hr after Alexa568-MakA treatment.
source: The time scale of MakA binding to individual HCT8 cells ranged from ~40 min to 4 hr after Alexa568-MakA treatment (Figure 1F–H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by live-cell imaging data in Figure 1F–H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Alexa568-MakA was detected on the plasma membrane of the entire cell population, with most cells positive for tubular structures protruding out from the plasma membrane.
source: Ultimately, Alexa568-MakA was detected on the plasma membrane of the entire cell population, with most cells positive for tubular structures protruding out from the plasma membrane (Figure 1F–H).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by microscopy images in Figure 1F–H.

claim: MakA can cause tubulation of both endolysosomal membranes and plasma membranes in a pH-dependent manner.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that MakA can cause tubulation of both endolysosomal membranes and plasma membranes in a pH-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental findings presented in the Results section.

claim: MakA bound to HCT8 epithelial cells in a pH-dependent manner.
source: To further assess the effect of pH on the binding of MakA to HCT8 epithelial cells, we performed Western blot analysis using anti-MakA antiserum (Figure 2A). We observed that MakA bound to the cells in a pH-dependent manner and that there seemed to be a pH-dependent formation of stable MakA oligomers bound to the epithelial cells.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by Western blot data in Figure 2A.

claim: There was a pH-dependent formation of stable MakA oligomers bound to the epithelial cells.
source: We observed that MakA bound to the cells in a pH-dependent manner and that there seemed to be a pH-dependent formation of stable MakA oligomers bound to the epithelial cells.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by Western blot data in Figure 2A.

claim: MakA caused pH-dependent toxicity of HCT8 cells.
source: In addition to causing pH-dependent toxicity of HCT8 cells, MakA was similarly toxic to other colon cancer cells, Caco-2 and HCT116 cells, as revealed by an increase in the number of trypan blue-positive cells in response to an increasing concentration of MakA in low pH conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by propidium iodide uptake assays in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: MakA was similarly toxic to Caco-2 and HCT116 cells as revealed by an increase in the number of trypan blue-positive cells in response to an increasing concentration of MakA in low pH conditions.
source: In addition to causing pH-dependent toxicity of HCT8 cells, MakA was similarly toxic to other colon cancer cells, Caco-2 and HCT116 cells, as revealed by an increase in the number of trypan blue-positive cells in response to an increasing concentration of MakA in low pH conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by trypan blue exclusion assays in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: When erythrocytes were exposed to MakA at pH 5.0, hemolysis was observed in a concentration-dependent manner within 90 min.
source: When erythrocytes were exposed to MakA at pH 5.0, hemolysis was observed in a concentration-dependent manner within 90 min (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by hemolysis assay data in Figure 2C.

claim: MakA failed to induce hemolysis of erythrocytes at pH 6.5 or pH 7.4 during the 90 min treatment.
source: In contrast, MakA failed to induce hemolysis of erythrocytes at pH 6.5 or pH 7.4 during the 90 min treatment.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by hemolysis assay data in Figure 2C.

claim: A detectable, but low level of hemolysis was observed after 5 hr with erythrocytes exposed to MakA at pH 6.5.
source: A detectable, but low level of hemolysis was observed after 5 hr with erythrocytes exposed to MakA at pH 6.5 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by hemolysis assay data in Figure 2C.

claim: pH-dependent binding of Alexa568-MakA to erythrocytes was observed by confocal microscopy.
source: With confocal microscopy, we observed pH-dependent binding of Alexa568-MakA to erythrocytes. A majority of erythrocytes at pH 5.0 and 6.5 were covered by Alexa568-MakA, whereas there was virtually no MakA binding observed at pH 7.4 (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by confocal microscopy images in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A majority of erythrocytes at pH 5.0 and 6.5 were covered by Alexa568-MakA.
source: A majority of erythrocytes at pH 5.0 and 6.5 were covered by Alexa568-MakA, whereas there was virtually no MakA binding observed at pH 7.4 (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by confocal microscopy images in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There was virtually no MakA binding observed to erythrocytes at pH 7.4.
source: A majority of erythrocytes at pH 5.0 and 6.5 were covered by Alexa568-MakA, whereas there was virtually no MakA binding observed at pH 7.4 (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by confocal microscopy images in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Tubular structures were detected in association with MakA at the red blood cell surface.
source: Notably, we detected the presence of tubular structures in association with MakA at the red blood cell surface, as shown by a maximum 3D projection of the z-stack images of erythrocytes (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by confocal microscopy images in Figure 2E.

claim: The presence of MakA-induced tubular structures on the surface of erythrocytes was observed by TEM and scanning electron microscopy (SEM).
source: The presence of MakA-induced tubular structures on the surface of erythrocytes was further observed by TEM and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (Figure 2F and G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by TEM and SEM images in Figure 2F and G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: MakA could accumulate in a pH-dependent manner at the surface of both epithelial cells and erythrocytes, thereby inducing formation of tubular structures that ultimately lead to cell lysis.
source: Together, these results suggest that MakA could accumulate in a pH-dependent manner at the surface of both epithelial cells and erythrocytes, thereby inducing formation of tubular structures that ultimately lead to cell lysis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental findings presented in the Results section.

claim: More MakA was associated with ECLE liposomes at pH 5.0 and 6.5 than at pH 7.4.
source: After the addition of MakA, the liposomes were pelleted by centrifugation and the presence of MakA in either the pellet or the supernatant was detected by Western blot analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A). The results indicated that more MakA was associated with the liposomes at pH 5.0 and 6.5 than at pH 7.4.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by Western blot data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the absence of liposomes, the CD spectra indicated a decrease in the α-helical content of MakA protein when in an acidic environment.
source: In the absence of liposomes, the CD spectra indicated a decrease in the α-helical content of the protein when in an acidic environment.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by CD spectroscopy data in Figure 3A.

claim: The decrease in α-helical content of MakA was restored when ECLE liposomes were present, suggesting that liposomes somehow stabilized the structure of MakA.
source: This decrease in α-helical content of MakA was restored when ECLE liposomes were present, suggesting that liposomes somehow stabilized the structure of MakA (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by CD spectroscopy data in Figure 3A and B.

claim: TEM analysis of MakA at different pH indicated that it formed oligomeric structures in a pH-dependent manner.
source: TEM analysis of MakA at different pH indicated that it formed oligomeric structures in a pH-dependent manner (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by TEM images in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MakA triggered tubulation of the ECLE liposomes in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: In a similar manner to the tubulation observed for the target cell membranes and lysosomes, MakA triggered tubulation of the ECLE liposomes in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by TEM images in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Concomitant with the assembly of tubular structures emanating from the liposomes, size of the liposomes appeared to shrink as the tubules grew up to several micrometers in length.
source: Concomitant with the assembly of tubular structures emanating from the liposomes, size of the liposomes appeared to shrink as the tubules grew up to several micrometers in length.
evidence: This is a primary experimental observation supported by TEM images in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The entire liposome seemed to be transformed into long tubules.
source: Ultimately, the entire liposome seemed to be transformed into long tubules (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental observation supported by TEM and confocal microscopy images in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: Tubulation of ECLE liposomes was also observed by confocal microscopy upon treatment with Alexa568-labeled MakA.
source: The tubulation of ECLE liposomes was also observed by confocal microscopy upon treatment with Alexa568-labeled MakA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by confocal microscopy images in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: In the same population of small liposome particles, Alexa568-MakA-positive large lipid vesicles (5–10 μm in size, less than 1% of the entire liposome fraction) were detected.
source: In the same population of small liposome particles, we also detected Alexa568-MakA-positive large lipid vesicles (5–10 μm in size, less than 1% of the entire liposome fraction).
evidence: This is a primary experimental observation supported by confocal microscopy data.

claim: The z-stack projection suggested that the whole lipid vesicle was decorated with a bundle of fluctuating tubules.
source: The z-stack projection suggested that the whole lipid vesicle was decorated with a bundle of fluctuating tubules (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a primary experimental observation supported by confocal microscopy images in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Tubulation of the SLM liposomes by MakA was observed by TEM.
source: Tubulation of the SLM liposomes by MakA was observed by TEM (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by TEM images in Figure 3C.

claim: A large number of well-organized, star-shaped oligomeric particles of MakA were observed among the ECLE liposomes.
source: In addition to the tubular structures, we observed a large number of well-organized, star-shaped oligomeric particles of MakA among the ECLE liposomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a primary experimental observation supported by TEM images in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The presence of MakA protein in the tubular structures was evidenced by immunogold staining using MakA-specific antiserum.
source: Furthermore, the presence of MakA protein in the tubular structures was evidenced by immunogold staining using MakA-specific antiserum (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by immunogold TEM images in Figure 3D.

claim: By fluorescence microscopy, tube growth originating from a supported lipid bilayer (SLB) prepared from SLM liposomes containing the fluorescent lipid Texas Red-DHPE was visualized, demonstrating that the tubes also contain lipids from the SLB.
source: By fluorescence microscopy, we were able to visualize tube growth originating from a supported lipid bilayer (SLB) prepared from SLM liposomes containing the fluorescent lipid Texas Red-DHPE, demonstrating that the tubes also contain lipids from the SLB (Figure 3E and Video 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by fluorescence microscopy images in Figure 3E and Video 1.

claim: Administering Alexa568-MakA to an SLB prepared from SLM liposomes prompted a significant and highly dynamic membrane remodeling.
source: Using fluorescence microscopy, we found that administering Alexa568-MakA to an SLB prepared from SLM liposomes prompted a significant and highly dynamic membrane remodeling (Figure 3F and Video 2).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by fluorescence microscopy images in Figure 3F and Video 2.

claim: Within 10 min, Alexa568-MakA binding to the SLBs resulted in formation of MakA-associated tubules of various sizes.
source: Within 10 min, Alexa568-MakA binding to the SLBs resulted in formation of MakA-associated tubules of various sizes (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by fluorescence microscopy images in Figure 3F.

claim: At pH 6.5 or lower, MakA may adopt a conformation that allows the protein to insert into the lipid membrane in the form of an oligomer assembly that can lead to the formation of a tube structure.
source: Based on these findings, we propose that at pH 6.5 or lower, MakA may adopt a conformation that allows the protein to insert into the lipid membrane in the form of an oligomer assembly that can lead to the formation of a tube structure.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on experimental findings.

claim: Concomitantly, the size of the vesicle appears to shrink, and the tube may grow up to several micrometers in length.
source: Concomitantly, the size of the vesicle appears to shrink, and the tube may grow up to several micrometers in length.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on experimental observations.

claim: The MakA-lipid tubulation can occur without the involvement of other proteins or some specific protein receptor under the pH conditions tested.
source: Our results suggest that the MakA-lipid tubulation can occur without the involvement of other proteins or some specific protein receptor under the pH conditions tested.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments with protein-free liposomes.

claim: An initial 2D classification allowed identification of repetitive elements and measurement of a helical repeat distance of ~216 Å.
source: An initial 2D classification allowed us to identify repetitive elements and measure a helical repeat distance of ~216 Å (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from cryo-EM structural analysis supported by data in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: One repeating element of the right-handed spiral consists of 37 tetramers that complete five turns around the helical axis, spanning a length of 216.5 Å and a diameter of 322 Å.
source: One repeating element of the right-handed spiral consists of 37 tetramers that complete five turns around the helical axis, spanning a length of 216.5 Å and a diameter of 322 Å.
evidence: This is a primary finding from cryo-EM structural analysis.

claim: This arrangement results in an axial rise of 5.85 Å per subunit and a helical twist of 48.65°.
source: This arrangement results in an axial rise of 5.85 Å per subunit and a helical twist of 48.65° (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from cryo-EM structural analysis supported by data in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Application of the initially calculated helical symmetry values with local searches in a 3D refinement resulted in a cryo-EM map at an overall resolution of 3.7 Å.
source: Application of these initially calculated values with local searches in a 3D refinement further optimized symmetry parameters and resulted in a cryo-EM map at an overall resolution of 3.7 Å (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A-D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from cryo-EM structural analysis supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A-D.

claim: The obtained cryo-EM map features a well-resolved central transmembrane helix (TMH) region and a less well-resolved peripheral region.
source: The obtained cryo-EM map features a well-resolved central transmembrane helix (TMH) region and a less well-resolved peripheral region (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from cryo-EM structural analysis supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: The clear connectivity of the obtained density map allowed for reliable secondary structure placement using the MakA soluble state crystal structure (PDB-6EZV).
source: The clear connectivity of the obtained density map (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 3E) allowed for reliable secondary structure placement using the MakA soluble state crystal structure (PDB-6EZV, Dongre et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a primary finding from cryo-EM structural analysis supported by data in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 3E, and using the crystal structure from Dongre et al., 2018.

claim: High-resolution features in the helical reconstruction allowed for de novo model building of structural elements in the central region.
source: High-resolution features in the helical reconstruction (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 3F) allowed for de novo model building of structural elements in the central region.
evidence: This is a primary finding from cryo-EM structural analysis supported by data in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 3F.

claim: Due to continuous rotation along the filament axis, flexibility, and the conformational difference with respect to the crystal structure, the MakA tail domain structure is less reliable and modeled with poly-alanine secondary structure elements.
source: However, due to continuous rotation along the filament axis, flexibility (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and the conformational difference with respect to the crystal structure, the MakA tail domain structure is less reliable and modeled with poly-alanine secondary structure elements.
evidence: This is a limitation of the structural analysis explained by the authors, supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: MakA oligomerizes into a filamentous structure growing from or ending in membranous vesicles.
source: MakA oligomerizes into a filamentous structure growing from or ending in membranous vesicles (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from cryo-EM analysis supported by micrographs in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The building blocks of the MakA filament are formed by two MakA dimers.
source: The building blocks of this filament are formed by two MakA dimers (Figure 4B and D) that organize into a pinecone-like architecture, spiraling around a central cavity (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from cryo-EM structural analysis supported by data in Figure 4B, C, and D.

claim: The MakA helix features a propeller-like structure with a weak, annular density embedded in-between the blades formed by MakA from the top view along the filament axis.
source: From the top view along the filament axis, the helix features a propeller-like structure with a weak, annular density embedded in-between the blades formed by MakA (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from cryo-EM structural analysis supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: The annular density resembles lipid tails and contains some spherical features, which could be associated with phospholipid heads, suggesting the presence of a thin phospholipid bilayer that spirals around the central cavity of the filament.
source: This density resembles lipid tails and contains some spherical features, which could be associated with phospholipid heads, suggesting the presence of a thin phospholipid bilayer that spirals around the central cavity of the filament (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from cryo-EM structural analysis supported by data in Figure 4C.

claim: The annular density is located between the TMHs of MakA, indicating that the active toxin form interacts with lipid vesicles and starts to oligomerize by internalizing membrane lipids.
source: Interestingly, the annular density is located between the TMHs of MakA (Figure 4D), indicating that the active toxin form interacts with lipid vesicles and starts to oligomerize by internalizing membrane lipids.
evidence: This is a primary finding from cryo-EM structural analysis supported by data in Figure 4D.

claim: The basic building block of the observed protein-lipid filament is formed by four MakA subunits in a membrane-bound active conformation.
source: The basic building block of the observed protein-lipid filament is formed by four MakA subunits in a membrane-bound active conformation (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from cryo-EM structural analysis supported by data in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The membrane-bound conformation of MakA is significantly different from the previously reported soluble state structures resembling the inactive form (PDB-6DFP and PDB-6EZV).
source: This conformation of MakA is significantly different from the previously reported soluble state structures resembling the inactive form (PDB-6DFP and PDB-6EZV, Dongre et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a primary finding from cryo-EM structural analysis compared to previously published crystal structures from Dongre et al., 2018.

claim: In the soluble form, a C-terminal tail (res. 351–365) inactivates the predicted transmembrane domains by forming a β-tongue, consisting of three β-sheets, that shields the hydrophobic residues from the surrounding solvent.
source: In the soluble form, a C-terminal tail (res. 351–365, Figure 5C, purple) inactivates the predicted transmembrane domains by forming a β-tongue, consisting of three β-sheets (Dongre et al., 2018), that shields the hydrophobic residues from the surrounding solvent.
evidence: This is a description of the soluble form structure supported by the crystal structure from Dongre et al., 2018 and illustrated in Figure 5C.

claim: This shielding characteristic is well described for the soluble form of the ClyA PFT family, including ClyA, Hbl-B, NheA, and AhlB.
source: This shielding characteristic is well described for the soluble form of the ClyA PFT family, including ClyA, Hbl-B, NheA, and AhlB (Ganash et al., 2013; Kovac et al., 2016; Madegowda et al., 2008; Schubert et al., 2018; Wallace et al., 2000; Wilson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ganash et al., 2013; Kovac et al., 2016; Madegowda et al., 2008; Schubert et al., 2018; Wallace et al., 2000; and Wilson et al., 2019.

claim: MakA undergoes a structural change comparable to the opening of a Swiss army knife blade when it shifts from a soluble inactive to a membrane-bound active state.
source: MakA undergoes a structural change comparable to the opening of a Swiss army knife blade when it shifts from a soluble inactive to a membrane-bound active state, where the helix bundle of the tail region represents the handle, the transition from the tail to the neck region forms two hinges, and the β-tongue together with 4 and 5 resembles the blade that folds out (Figure 5C, α4 and α5; light and dark green).
evidence: This is a primary finding from cryo-EM structural analysis comparing the membrane-bound and soluble forms, illustrated in Figure 5C.

claim: The β-tongue changes its secondary structure and, together with α4 and α5/α6, forms two extended helices.
source: Additionally, the β-tongue changes its secondary structure and, together with α4 and α5/α6, forms two extended helices (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from cryo-EM structural analysis illustrated in Figure 5C.

claim: This significant conformational change leads to the formation of two TMHs and a short loop region (res. 219–221) between α4 and α5.
source: This significant conformational change leads to the formation of two TMHs and a short loop region (res. 219–221) between α4 and α5.
evidence: This is a primary finding from cryo-EM structural analysis.

claim: All four copies of MakA adopt different conformations within the tetramer.
source: Interestingly, despite certain similarities, all four copies of MakA adopt different conformations within the tetramer, as indicated by MakA-1 to MakA-4 (Figures 4 and 5).
evidence: This is a primary finding from cryo-EM structural analysis illustrated in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The most significant structural differences between the four MakA conformations can be observed in the neck and head domains, connected via a hinge with the tail domains.
source: The most significant structural differences between the four MakA conformations can be observed in the neck and head domains, connected via a hinge with the tail domains (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from cryo-EM structural analysis illustrated in Figure 5C.

claim: The hinge allows for different degrees of bending (opening up of the Swiss army knife), while the neck helices α4 and α5 and the loop region (res. 219–221) display a high degree of plasticity.
source: The hinge allows for different degrees of bending (opening up of the Swiss army knife), while the neck helices α4 and α5 and the loop region (res. 219–221) display a high degree of plasticity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from cryo-EM structural analysis.

claim: For the peripheral tail domain, two major conformations can be observed: in MakA-2 and MakA-4, this region superimposes well with the crystal structure, whereas helix α6 of MakA-1 and MakA-3 moves by almost 10 Å to extend the length of α5.
source: For the peripheral tail domain, two major conformations can be observed. In MakA-2 and MakA-4, this region superimposes well with the crystal structure, whereas helix α6 of MakA-1 and MakA-3 moves by almost 10 Å to extend the length of α5.
evidence: This is a primary finding from cryo-EM structural analysis.

claim: While the stretched MakA states have shorter N-terminal helices than the kinked MakA forms, the C-terminal β-strand (res. 351–365), which covers the TMH in the soluble state, is disordered in all four subunits.
source: While the stretched MakA states have shorter N-terminal helices than the kinked MakA forms, the C-terminal β-strand (res. 351–365), which covers the TMH in the soluble state, is disordered in all four subunits.
evidence: This is a primary finding from cryo-EM structural analysis.

claim: Different bacterial species, notably B. cereus, A. hydrophila, S. marcescens, and V. cholerae, have the capability to produce structurally similar tripartite protein complexes that assemble on host cell membranes as pore structures that are cytolytic.
source: Recent studies have revealed how different bacterial species, notably B. cereus, A. hydrophila, S. marcescens, and V. cholerae, have the capability to produce structurally similar tripartite protein complexes that assemble on host cell membranes as pore structures that are cytolytic (Churchill-Angus et al., 2021; Nadeem et al., 2021c; Sastalla et al., 2013; Wilson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Churchill-Angus et al., 2021; Nadeem et al., 2021c; Sastalla et al., 2013; and Wilson et al., 2019.

claim: The MakA component of the tripartite complex, when presented alone to mammalian cells, is effectively internalized and accumulates on endolysosomal membranes, leading to induction of autophagy and apoptotic cell death.
source: In the case of V. cholerae, it has become evident that the MakA component of the tripartite complex, when presented alone to mammalian cells, is effectively internalized and accumulates on endolysosomal membranes, leading to induction of autophagy and apoptotic cell death (Corkery et al., 2021; Nadeem et al., 2021a; Nadeem et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Corkery et al., 2021; Nadeem et al., 2021a; and Nadeem et al., 2021b.

claim: MakA can modulate host cell autophagy in a pH-dependent manner.
source: Moreover, MakA can modulate host cell autophagy in a pH-dependent manner (Corkery et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Corkery et al., 2021.

claim: MakA is able to produce a novel protein-lipid polymeric superstructure at a low pH (6.5 or below) that perturbs host cell membranes.
source: Herein, we show that MakA is able to produce a novel protein-lipid polymeric superstructure at a low pH (6.5 or below) that perturbs host cell membranes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the Discussion.

claim: Several prokaryotic proteins are known to polymerize in the presence of a matrix such as a lipid membrane or DNA.
source: Several prokaryotic proteins are known to polymerize in the presence of a matrix such as a lipid membrane or DNA.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge in the Discussion.

claim: This type of assembly is referred to as a collaborative filament.
source: This type of assembly is referred to as a collaborative filament (Ghosal and Löwe, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ghosal and Löwe, 2015.

claim: In the presence of lipid membranes, collaborative filaments are assembled by a bridging protein and lipid on the membrane in a sequence-specific manner and by sensing membrane curvature.
source: In the presence of lipid membranes, collaborative filaments are assembled by a bridging protein and lipid on the membrane in a sequence-specific manner and by sensing membrane curvature (Ghosal and Löwe, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ghosal and Löwe, 2015.

claim: Membrane-mediated clustering of Shiga toxin molecules and the formation of tubular membrane invaginations are essential steps in the clathrin-independent Shiga toxin uptake process.
source: It was demonstrated that membrane-mediated clustering of Shiga toxin molecules and the formation of tubular membrane invaginations are essential steps in the clathrin-independent Shiga toxin uptake process (Pezeshkian et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pezeshkian et al., 2016.

claim: pH-dependent membrane insertion and increased cytotoxic activity were demonstrated for different bacterial toxins, including anthrax toxin from Bacillus anthracis, diphtheria toxin from Corynebacterium diphtheriae, VacA from Helicobacter pylori, perfringolysin from Clostridium perfringens, and listeriolysin O from Listeria monocytogenes.
source: In earlier studies, pH-dependent membrane insertion and increased cytotoxic activity were demonstrated for different bacterial toxins, including anthrax toxin from Bacillus anthracis (Koehler and Collier, 1991), diphtheria toxin from Corynebacterium diphtheriae (Rodnin et al., 2016), VacA from Helicobacter pylori (Pagliaccia et al., 2000), perfringolysin from Clostridium perfringens (Nelson et al., 2008), and listeriolysin O from Listeria monocytogenes (Schuerch et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Koehler and Collier, 1991; Rodnin et al., 2016; Pagliaccia et al., 2000; Nelson et al., 2008; and Schuerch et al., 2005.

claim: Pre-pore-to-pore transformation of mammalian perforin 2 (mPFN2) occurs at an acidic pH, which is accomplished by a 180° rotation of the membrane-attacking domain and β-hairpin P2 domain with respect to one another, allowing membrane insertion to take place.
source: Recent research on the pre- and pore forms of a mammalian PFT, the protein perforin 2 (mPFN2), provides interesting insights into the pore generation process. It was demonstrated that pre-pore-to-pore transformation occurs at an acidic pH, which is accomplished by a 180° rotation of the membrane-attacking domain and β-hairpin P2 domain with respect to one another, allowing membrane insertion to take place (Ni et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ni et al., 2020.

claim: A decrease in pH facilitated the MakA structural change comparable to the opening of a Swiss army knife blade when shifting from a soluble to a membrane-bound active state that interacts with the lipid membrane.
source: Similar to these other toxins, a decrease in pH facilitated the MakA structural change comparable to the opening of a Swiss army knife blade when shifting from a soluble to a membrane-bound active state that interacts with the lipid membrane.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural analysis and comparison to other toxins.

claim: The pH-induced structural change potentiated the MakA-induced cytotoxic effect on the target cell under the conditions tested.
source: The pH-induced structural change potentiated the MakA-induced cytotoxic effect on the target cell under the conditions tested.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: MakA co-localizes with β-catenin, actin, and the phosphatidic acid biosensor, PASS, in filipodia-rich structures.
source: Consistent with these results, we recently found that MakA co-localizes with β-catenin, actin, and the phosphatidic acid biosensor, PASS, in filipodia-rich structures (Nadeem et al., 2021a; Nadeem et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nadeem et al., 2021a and Nadeem et al., 2021b.

claim: Low pH enhanced the activity of MakA, characterized by a striking tubulation of both purified lysosomes and liposomes prepared from ECLE.
source: In all model systems, we observed that low pH enhanced the activity of MakA, characterized by a striking tubulation of both purified lysosomes and liposomes prepared from ECLE.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental findings.

claim: MakA formed tubular structures on liposomes independent of any specific protein receptor or energy-generating molecules, that is, ATP or GTP.
source: Furthermore, it was found that MakA formed tubular structures on liposomes independent of any specific protein receptor or energy-generating molecules, that is, ATP or GTP, suggesting that at low pH, the structural change and insertion of MakA itself was sufficient to trigger tubulation at the membrane surface.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments with protein-free liposomes.

claim: At low pH, the structural change and insertion of MakA itself was sufficient to trigger tubulation at the membrane surface.
source: Furthermore, it was found that MakA formed tubular structures on liposomes independent of any specific protein receptor or energy-generating molecules, that is, ATP or GTP, suggesting that at low pH, the structural change and insertion of MakA itself was sufficient to trigger tubulation at the membrane surface.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments with protein-free liposomes.

claim: MakA could induce tubulation on liposomes obtained from lipid sources essentially lacking cholesterol, that is, E. coli and C. elegans.
source: In contrast to some other PFTs that need cholesterol for oligomerization (Gellings and McGee, 2018; Rosado et al., 2008; Sathyanarayana et al., 2018), MakA could induce tubulation on liposomes obtained from lipid sources essentially lacking cholesterol, that is, E. coli and C. elegans, showing that the pH-dependent tubulation of MakA can occur in the absence of cholesterol in the membrane.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by TEM images in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: The pH-dependent tubulation of MakA can occur in the absence of cholesterol in the membrane.
source: In contrast to some other PFTs that need cholesterol for oligomerization (Gellings and McGee, 2018; Rosado et al., 2008; Sathyanarayana et al., 2018), MakA could induce tubulation on liposomes obtained from lipid sources essentially lacking cholesterol, that is, E. coli and C. elegans, showing that the pH-dependent tubulation of MakA can occur in the absence of cholesterol in the membrane.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments with cholesterol-free liposomes.

claim: Bacterial cell membranes are typically devoid of cholesterol.
source: Bacterial cell membranes are typically devoid of cholesterol (Fiertel and Klein, 1959), while the membranes of C. elegans are mostly composed of glycerophospholipids and sphingolipids with trace quantities of cholesterol (Watts and Ristow, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fiertel and Klein, 1959.

claim: The membranes of C. elegans are mostly composed of glycerophospholipids and sphingolipids with trace quantities of cholesterol.
source: Bacterial cell membranes are typically devoid of cholesterol (Fiertel and Klein, 1959), while the membranes of C. elegans are mostly composed of glycerophospholipids and sphingolipids with trace quantities of cholesterol (Watts and Ristow, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Watts and Ristow, 2017.

claim: The presence of cholesterol was not required for the oligomerization of MakA in solution.
source: In addition, we observed that the presence of cholesterol was not required for the oligomerization of MakA in solution (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by TEM images in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The in vitro studies do not indicate that a particular membrane topology per se is required for the MakA-induced tube formation.
source: Importantly, our in vitro studies do not indicate that a particular membrane topology per se is required for the MakA-induced tube formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: MakA can interact with membrane lipids representing either side or topology of a membrane bilayer and thereby induce tubulation when the pH is acidic.
source: The data indicate that MakA can interact with membrane lipids representing either side or topology of a membrane bilayer and thereby induce tubulation when the pH is acidic.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Shiga toxin and CT insert into the membrane and cause inward-directed tubulations of artificial lipid membranes since toxin binding induces negative curvature of the plasma membrane.
source: This membrane interaction by MakA thereby appears different from, for example, Shiga toxin and CT, which insert into the membrane and cause inward-directed tubulations of artificial lipid membranes since toxin binding induces negative curvature of the plasma membrane (Chinnapen et al., 2012; Römer et al., 2007; Safouane et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chinnapen et al., 2012; Römer et al., 2007; and Safouane et al., 2010.

claim: Under acidic conditions MakA undergoes a conformational change, presumably adopting a structure that is promoting membrane interaction and formation of oligomeric assemblies.
source: The CD spectrometry and TEM-negative staining data indicate that under acidic conditions MakA undergoes a conformational change, presumably adopting a structure that is promoting membrane interaction and formation of oligomeric assemblies (Figure 2A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from CD spectroscopy and TEM data in Figure 2A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MakA evidently drives the rapid growth of tubules toward the extracellular space, as shown with red blood cells.
source: MakA evidently drives the rapid growth of tubules toward the extracellular space, as shown with red blood cells (Figure 2E-G).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by microscopy images in Figure 2E-G.

claim: The appearance of tubular structures in response to MakA was a direct consequence of MakA insertion into the membrane, which appeared to create the conditions for generating a positive curvature.
source: We propose that the appearance of tubular structures in response to MakA was a direct consequence of MakA insertion into the membrane, which appeared to create the conditions for generating a positive curvature, as described previously for protein-lipid complexes and multi-anchoring polymers (Campelo, 2007; Nadeem et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on experimental findings and supported by citations to Campelo, 2007 and Nadeem et al., 2015.

claim: MakA and ESCRT-III proteins seem to have some similarities in terms of the major refolding of the subunit with ESCRT-III proteins.
source: MakA and ESCRT-III proteins seem to have some similarities in terms of the major refolding of the subunit with ESCRT-III proteins.
evidence: This is a comparison made in the Discussion.

claim: Both MakA and ESCRT-III proteins tubulate membranes ultrastructurally.
source: Both proteins tubulate membranes ultrastructurally and, as observed for MakA, human ESCRT-III protein CHMP1B/IST1 generates a positive membrane curvature (Nguyen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparison made in the Discussion and supported by a citation to Nguyen et al., 2020.

claim: Human ESCRT-III protein CHMP1B/IST1 generates a positive membrane curvature.
source: Both proteins tubulate membranes ultrastructurally and, as observed for MakA, human ESCRT-III protein CHMP1B/IST1 generates a positive membrane curvature (Nguyen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nguyen et al., 2020.

claim: CHMP1B proteins associate with and coat a membrane externally through positively charged phospholipid-interacting regions in helix 1, resulting in a stable, continuous, and intact membrane.
source: However, there are major differences between the proteins in terms of membrane interaction and oligomeric assembly: Through positively charged phospholipid-interacting regions in helix 1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 4, shown in red), CHMP1B proteins associate with and coat a membrane externally, resulting in a stable, continuous, and intact membrane.
evidence: This is a comparison made in the Discussion and illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: MakA has transmembrane domains that integrate into and span the lipid bilayer.
source: MakA, on the other hand, has transmembrane domains that integrate into and span the lipid bilayer.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the structural analysis.

claim: When the membrane is disassembled and linearized, a lipid spiral forms around the filament axis, together with the MakA subunits.
source: When the membrane is disassembled and linearized, a lipid spiral forms around the filament axis, together with the MakA subunits.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the structural analysis.

claim: The lipid spiral formation implies membrane instability, which is consistent with the proposed cytotoxicity of MakA as opposed to ESCRT-III-regulated membrane remodeling and fission.
source: This implies membrane instability, which is consistent with the proposed cytotoxicity of MakA as opposed to ESCRT-III-regulated membrane remodeling and fission.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural analysis and comparison to ESCRT-III.

claim: Reduced ionic strength activates ESCRT-III.
source: Moreover, reduced ionic strength activates ESCRT-III (McCullough et al., 2015), whereas the trigger for MakA appears to be pH dependent.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McCullough et al., 2015.

claim: The trigger for MakA appears to be pH dependent.
source: Moreover, reduced ionic strength activates ESCRT-III (McCullough et al., 2015), whereas the trigger for MakA appears to be pH dependent.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: CHMP1B in its open, active conformation needs its binding partner, IST1, to co-polymerize and promote membrane tubulation.
source: CHMP1B in its open, active conformation needs its binding partner, IST1, to co-polymerize and promote membrane tubulation (McCullough et al., 2015), while MakA oligomerizes into a helical filament on its own in vitro (by forming pairs of dimers).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McCullough et al., 2015.

claim: MakA oligomerizes into a helical filament on its own in vitro (by forming pairs of dimers).
source: CHMP1B in its open, active conformation needs its binding partner, IST1, to co-polymerize and promote membrane tubulation (McCullough et al., 2015), while MakA oligomerizes into a helical filament on its own in vitro (by forming pairs of dimers).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the structural analysis.

claim: When MakA is interacting in vitro with its other binding partners from V. cholerae, the structurally related MakB and MakE proteins, it acts as a component in a tripartite complex, forming oligomeric pore structures in membranes at neutral pH.
source: It should be noted that when MakA is interacting in vitro with its other binding partners from V. cholerae, the structurally related MakB and MakE proteins, it acts as a component in a tripartite complex, forming oligomeric pore structures in membranes at neutral pH (Nadeem et al., 2021c).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nadeem et al., 2021c.

claim: The observed structural heterogeneity within the dimer pair of MakA shown at acidic pH presumably reflects its ability to engage in heteromeric interactions with the other two Mak proteins.
source: The observed structural heterogeneity within the dimer pair of MakA shown at acidic pH in the present study presumably reflects its ability to engage in heteromeric interactions with the other two Mak proteins.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for the structural heterogeneity observed in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Oligomerized CHMP1B and MakA have dramatically different protein-protein interactions: MakA creates pairs of dimers that are arrayed like a single propellor blade, while CHMP1B binds to four successive CHMP1B monomers that are almost parallel packed next to each other, resulting in a low-fence-like structure.
source: Furthermore, oligomerized CHMP1B and MakA have dramatically different protein-protein interactions: MakA creates pairs of dimers that are arrayed like a single propellor blade, while CHMP1B binds to four successive CHMP1B monomers that are almost parallel packed next to each other, resulting in a low-fence-like structure (McCullough et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison made in the Discussion and supported by a citation to McCullough et al., 2015.

claim: Within the oligomerized MakA filament, the TMHs line the inner cavity, interacting with lipids that are intercalated both within the dimer interface and between the dimers in the helical spiral.
source: Within the oligomerized MakA filament, the TMHs line the inner cavity, interacting with lipids that are intercalated both within the dimer interface and between the dimers in the helical spiral (Figures 4C and 5B).
